claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) in elderly adds substantially to socioeconomic burden necessitating early diagnosis.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) in elderly adds substantially to socioeconomic burden necessitating early diagnosis.
evidence: This is a general statement about AD's impact, drawing from established scientific consensus about the disease's burden.

claim: Recent studies in rodent models of AD have suggested diagnostic and therapeutic value for gamma rhythms in brain.
source: While recent studies in rodent models of AD have suggested diagnostic and therapeutic value for gamma rhythms in brain, the same has not been rigorously tested in humans.
evidence: This claim references prior research in rodent models, which is supported by citations in the Introduction section.

claim: Stimulus-induced gamma rhythms have not been rigorously tested in humans with AD.
source: While recent studies in rodent models of AD have suggested diagnostic and therapeutic value for gamma rhythms in brain, the same has not been rigorously tested in humans.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: The study recruited a large population (N = 244; 106 females) of elderly (>49 years) subjects from the community.
source: In this case-control study, we recruited a large population (N = 244; 106 females) of elderly (>49 years) subjects from the community, who viewed large gratings that induced strong gamma oscillations in their electroencephalogram (EEG).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's sample size and demographics.

claim: Subjects viewed large gratings that induced strong gamma oscillations in their electroencephalogram (EEG).
source: In this case-control study, we recruited a large population (N = 244; 106 females) of elderly (>49 years) subjects from the community, who viewed large gratings that induced strong gamma oscillations in their electroencephalogram (EEG).
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm used in the study.

claim: Subjects were classified as healthy (N = 227), mild cognitively impaired (MCI; N = 12), or AD (N = 5) based on clinical history and Clinical Dementia Rating scores.
source: These subjects were classified as healthy (N = 227), mild cognitively impaired (MCI; N = 12), or AD (N = 5) based on clinical history and Clinical Dementia Rating scores.
evidence: This describes the classification criteria and sample sizes for each group.

claim: Stimulus-induced gamma rhythms were significantly lower in MCI/AD subjects compared to their age- and gender-matched controls.
source: Surprisingly, stimulus-induced gamma rhythms, but not alpha or steady-state visually evoked responses, were significantly lower in MCI/AD subjects compared to their age- and gender-matched controls.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: Alpha rhythms were not significantly different between MCI/AD subjects and controls.
source: Surprisingly, stimulus-induced gamma rhythms, but not alpha or steady-state visually evoked responses, were significantly lower in MCI/AD subjects compared to their age- and gender-matched controls.
evidence: This is stated as a negative finding in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Steady-state visually evoked responses were not significantly different between MCI/AD subjects and controls.
source: Surprisingly, stimulus-induced gamma rhythms, but not alpha or steady-state visually evoked responses, were significantly lower in MCI/AD subjects compared to their age- and gender-matched controls.
evidence: This is stated as a negative finding in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The reduction in gamma rhythms was not due to differences in eye movements.
source: This reduction was not due to differences in eye movements or baseline power.
evidence: This is supported by eye tracking data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The reduction in gamma rhythms was not due to differences in baseline power.
source: This reduction was not due to differences in eye movements or baseline power.
evidence: This is supported by baseline power analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Gamma could be used as a potential screening tool for MCI/AD in humans.
source: Our results suggest that gamma could be used as a potential screening tool for MCI/AD in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, representing an inference about potential applications.

claim: Gamma rhythms are narrow-band oscillations in brain's electrical activity with center frequency occupying ~30–80 Hz frequency range.
source: Gamma rhythms are narrow-band oscillations in brain's electrical activity with center frequency occupying ~30–80 Hz frequency range (Gray et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Gamma rhythms are suggested to be generated from excitatory-inhibitory interactions of pyramidal cell-interneuron networks.
source: These are suggested to be generated from excitatory-inhibitory interactions of pyramidal cell-interneuron networks (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012) involving parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) interneurons (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Gamma rhythms involve parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) interneurons.
source: These are suggested to be generated from excitatory-inhibitory interactions of pyramidal cell-interneuron networks (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012) involving parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) interneurons (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Gamma rhythms have been proposed to be involved in feature binding.
source: These have been proposed to be involved in certain cognitive functions like feature binding (Gray et al., 1989), attention (Chalk et al., 2010; Fries et al., 2001; Gregoriou et al., 2009), and working memory (Pesaran et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma rhythms have been proposed to be involved in attention.
source: These have been proposed to be involved in certain cognitive functions like feature binding (Gray et al., 1989), attention (Chalk et al., 2010; Fries et al., 2001; Gregoriou et al., 2009), and working memory (Pesaran et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Gamma rhythms have been proposed to be involved in working memory.
source: These have been proposed to be involved in certain cognitive functions like feature binding (Gray et al., 1989), attention (Chalk et al., 2010; Fries et al., 2001; Gregoriou et al., 2009), and working memory (Pesaran et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Verret et al., 2012 reported PV interneuron dysfunction in parietal cortex of AD patients and hAPP mice.
source: For example, Verret et al., 2012 reported PV interneuron dysfunction in parietal cortex of AD patients and hAPP mice (models of AD).
evidence: This is a direct reference to findings from a cited study.

claim: Verret et al., 2012 found aberrant gamma activity in parietal cortex in hAPP mice.
source: They found aberrant gamma activity in parietal cortex in such mice.
evidence: This is a direct reference to findings from a cited study.

claim: Iaccarino et al., 2016 suggested that visual stimulation using light flickering at 40 Hz entrained neural activity at 40 Hz and correlated with decrease in Aβ amyloid load in visual cortices of 5XFAD, APP/PS1 mice models of AD.
source: For example, Iaccarino et al., 2016 suggested that visual stimulation using light flickering at 40 Hz entrained neural activity at 40 Hz and correlated with decrease in Aβ amyloid load in visual cortices of 5XFAD, APP/PS1 mice models of AD.
evidence: This is a direct reference to findings from a cited study.

claim: Recent studies in human EEG have reported existence of two gamma rhythms (slow: ~20–34 Hz and fast: ~36–66 Hz) in visual cortex, elicited by Cartesian gratings.
source: Recent studies in human EEG (Murty et al., 2020; Murty et al., 2018) and MEG (Pantazis et al., 2018) have reported existence of two gamma rhythms (slow: ~20–34 Hz and fast: ~36–66 Hz) in visual cortex, elicited by Cartesian gratings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Age-related decline in power and/or frequency of stimulus-induced gamma rhythms has been shown in cognitively healthy subjects.
source: Age-related decline in power and/or frequency of these stimulus-induced gamma rhythms has been shown in cognitively healthy subjects (Gaetz et al., 2012; Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Abnormalities in stimulus-induced visual narrow-band gamma rhythms in human patients of MCI or AD have not been demonstrated till date.
source: However, abnormalities in such stimulus-induced visual narrow-band gamma rhythms in human patients of mild cognitive impairment (MCI, a preclinical stage of dementia [Albert et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 1999; Sosa et al., 2012]) or AD have not been demonstrated till date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: MCI is a preclinical stage of dementia.
source: However, abnormalities in such stimulus-induced visual narrow-band gamma rhythms in human patients of mild cognitive impairment (MCI, a preclinical stage of dementia [Albert et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 1999; Sosa et al., 2012]) or AD have not been demonstrated till date.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study monitored eyes using an infrared eye tracker to rule out differences in gamma power due to potential differences in eye position or microsaccade rate.
source: We monitored eyes using an infrared eye tracker to rule out differences in gamma power due to potential differences in eye position or microsaccade rate (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a methodological control used in the study.

claim: Gamma oscillations in EEG recorded from healthy young subjects have low orientation selectivity.
source: We have previously shown that gamma oscillations in EEG recorded from healthy young subjects have low orientation selectivity (Murty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Stimulus-induced change in fast gamma power did not vary significantly across different orientations in healthy subjects.
source: Consistent with this, we found that stimulus-induced change in fast gamma power did not vary significantly across different orientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; two-way ANOVA with spatial frequency and orientation as factors; F(3,2723) = 0.87, p=0.46) in healthy subjects, with very low orientation selectivity (mean ± SEM: 0.02 ± 0.002; see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data and reference to a figure.

claim: Slow gamma varied with orientation in healthy subjects.
source: Slow gamma varied with orientation (F(3,2723) = 6.4, p=0.0003); however, orientation selectivity calculated across the four orientations was small (mean ± SEM: 0.03 ± 0.002; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data and reference to a figure.

claim: Orientation selectivity for slow gamma calculated across the four orientations was small (mean ± SEM: 0.03 ± 0.002).
source: Slow gamma varied with orientation (F(3,2723) = 6.4, p=0.0003); however, orientation selectivity calculated across the four orientations was small (mean ± SEM: 0.03 ± 0.002; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Gamma power varied across spatial frequencies.
source: As reported previously, gamma power varied across spatial frequencies as well (same two-way ANOVA as above; slow/fast gamma: F(2,2723) = 31.1/50.7, p=4.6×10−14/2.4×10−22).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The difference in gamma between cases and controls was more prominent at spatial frequencies of 2 and 4 cpd.
source: In particular, we found that the difference in gamma between cases and controls was more prominent at spatial frequencies of 2 and 4 cpd, so we used the data for these two spatial frequencies for main analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from the data that guided the analysis strategy.

claim: Power in both slow gamma (20–34 Hz) and fast gamma (36–66 Hz) ranges was significantly lower in the MCI group compared to the control group.
source: While both slow and fast gamma 'bumps' were conspicuously visible for MCI as well as control groups, power in both slow gamma (20–34 Hz) and fast gamma (36–66 Hz) ranges (but not alpha, 8–12 Hz range) was significantly lower in the MCI group compared to the control group (Kruskal-Wallis [K-W] test, significance as shown in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is the main finding for the MCI group, supported by statistical analysis and reference to a figure.

claim: Alpha power (8–12 Hz range) was not significantly different between MCI and control groups.
source: While both slow and fast gamma 'bumps' were conspicuously visible for MCI as well as control groups, power in both slow gamma (20–34 Hz) and fast gamma (36–66 Hz) ranges (but not alpha, 8–12 Hz range) was significantly lower in the MCI group compared to the control group (Kruskal-Wallis [K-W] test, significance as shown in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a negative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Change in band-limited power was significantly less for both gamma bands in the MCI group compared to the control group (slow gamma: χ2(23) = 4.09, p=0.043; fast gamma: K-W test, χ2(23) = 5.61, p=0.018).
source: Change in band-limited power was significantly less for both gamma bands in the MCI group compared to the control group (Figure 2C; slow gamma: χ2(23) = 4.09, p=0.043; fast gamma: K-W test, χ2(23) = 5.61, p=0.018).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: Alpha power was not significantly different between MCI and control groups (χ2(23) = 0.33, p=0.56).
source: However, alpha power was not significantly different (χ2(23) = 0.33, p=0.56).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: Only 3/12 MCIs showed higher slow gamma power than controls.
source: Although there was substantial variability across subjects (also observed in Figure 2C), only 3/12 MCIs showed higher slow gamma power and only 2/12 MCIs showed higher fast gamma than controls.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data analysis.

claim: Only 2/12 MCIs showed higher fast gamma power than controls.
source: Although there was substantial variability across subjects (also observed in Figure 2C), only 3/12 MCIs showed higher slow gamma power and only 2/12 MCIs showed higher fast gamma than controls.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data analysis.

claim: Both slow and fast gamma were significantly reduced in AD subjects compared to controls (slow gamma: χ2(9) = 4.81 p=0.028; fast gamma: χ2(9) = 3.94, p=0.047).
source: We observed a strong reduction in the slow and fast gamma bands (Figure 3A and B), which was significant for both slow gamma (χ2(9) = 4.81 p=0.028) and fast gamma (χ2(9) = 3.94, p=0.047), but not alpha (χ2(9) = 0.01, p=0.92).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values for the AD group.

claim: Alpha power was not significantly different between AD subjects and controls (χ2(9) = 0.01, p=0.92).
source: We observed a strong reduction in the slow and fast gamma bands (Figure 3A and B), which was significant for both slow gamma (χ2(9) = 4.81 p=0.028) and fast gamma (χ2(9) = 3.94, p=0.047), but not alpha (χ2(9) = 0.01, p=0.92).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: All five AD subjects had less slow gamma power than controls.
source: All five AD subjects had less slow gamma power, and only one AD subject (A5) had more fast gamma power relative to the controls.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data analysis.

claim: Only one AD subject (A5) had more fast gamma power relative to the controls.
source: All five AD subjects had less slow gamma power, and only one AD subject (A5) had more fast gamma power relative to the controls.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data analysis.

claim: When MCI and AD data sets were combined, slow gamma (χ2(33) = 9.51, p=0.002) and fast gamma (χ2(33) = 8.88, p=0.003) power were strongly reduced in cases vs controls.
source: While slow gamma (χ2(33) = 9.51, p=0.002) and fast gamma (χ2(33) = 8.88, p=0.003) power were strongly reduced in cases vs controls, there was no difference in alpha power (χ2(33) = 0.25, p=0.61) or frequencies higher than ~65 Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values for the combined group.

claim: There was no difference in alpha power between combined MCI/AD cases and controls (χ2(33) = 0.25, p=0.61).
source: While slow gamma (χ2(33) = 9.51, p=0.002) and fast gamma (χ2(33) = 8.88, p=0.003) power were strongly reduced in cases vs controls, there was no difference in alpha power (χ2(33) = 0.25, p=0.61) or frequencies higher than ~65 Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: In the matched condition, the coefficient for CDR was significantly negative for both gamma bands (βCDR = –0.57/–0.25, p=0.0017/0.0063 for slow/fast gamma).
source: In the matched condition in which data from all the age- and gender-matched control subjects for each case were averaged (yielding 17 cases and 17 controls), the coefficient for CDR was significantly negative for both gamma bands (βCDR = –0.57/–0.25, p=0.0017/0.0063 for slow/fast gamma).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis showing the relationship between CDR and gamma power.

claim: In the unmatched condition, the CDR slope (βCDR) was significantly negative only for slow gamma (βCDR = –0.62/–0.29, p=0.0071/0.0702 for slow/fast gamma).
source: Results were similar for the unmatched condition, in which all the controls were considered separately (112 healthy, 12 MCI, and 6 AD subjects), albeit the CDR slope (βCDR) was significantly negative only for slow gamma (βCDR = –0.62/–0.29, p=0.0071/0.0702 for slow/fast gamma).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis showing the relationship between CDR and gamma power.

claim: Alpha power did not depend on CDR (βCDR = –0.30/–0.30, p=0.14/0.21 for matched/unmatched conditions).
source: On the other hand, similar to the results in previous analyses, alpha power did not depend on CDR (βCDR = –0.30/–0.30, p=0.14/0.21 for matched/unmatched conditions).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis.

claim: Gamma power decreases with age in healthy elderly.
source: We have previously shown that gamma power decreases with age in healthy elderly, and females have more gamma than males (Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Females have more gamma than males in healthy elderly.
source: We have previously shown that gamma power decreases with age in healthy elderly, and females have more gamma than males (Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The coefficient for age was significantly negative when regression analysis was performed on the full set of healthy subjects (N = 227) (βAGE = –0.018/–0.0094, p=0.014/0.06 for slow/fast gamma).
source: Consistent with these results, we found that coefficient for age was significantly negative (βAGE = –0.018/–0.0094, p=0.014/0.06 for slow/fast gamma), while coefficient for gender was significantly positive (βGENDER = 0.33/0.35, p=0.0070/3.15 × 10−5 for slow/fast gamma) when the regression analysis was performed on the full set of healthy subjects (N = 227).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis.

claim: The coefficient for gender was significantly positive when regression analysis was performed on the full set of healthy subjects (N = 227) (βGENDER = 0.33/0.35, p=0.0070/3.15 × 10−5 for slow/fast gamma).
source: Consistent with these results, we found that coefficient for age was significantly negative (βAGE = –0.018/–0.0094, p=0.014/0.06 for slow/fast gamma), while coefficient for gender was significantly positive (βGENDER = 0.33/0.35, p=0.0070/3.15 × 10−5 for slow/fast gamma) when the regression analysis was performed on the full set of healthy subjects (N = 227).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis.

claim: CDR is a stronger predictor of gamma power than age or gender.
source: This also suggests that CDR is a stronger predictor of gamma power than age or gender.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the regression analysis results.

claim: For the MCI group (N = 12), BF computed using single-tailed paired t-test was ~1.89 for both slow and fast gamma.
source: For the MCI group (N = 12), BF computed using single-tailed paired t-test was ~1.89 for both slow and fast gamma.
evidence: This is a result from Bayes factor analysis.

claim: Choosing a more 'sensitive' range for slow gamma (26–34 Hz) and fast gamma (44–56 Hz) improved the BF to 3.34 and 4.60, respectively, for the MCI group.
source: However, as before, choosing a more 'sensitive' range for slow gamma (26–34 Hz) and fast gamma (44–56 Hz) improved the BF to 3.34 and 4.60, respectively, suggesting substantial evidence for the alternate hypothesis over the null hypothesis.
evidence: This is a result from Bayes factor analysis with optimized frequency ranges.

claim: For the AD group (N = 5), BF was 2.85 for slow gamma and 1.83 for fast gamma.
source: For the AD group (N = 5), BF was 2.85 for slow gamma and 1.83 for fast gamma, suggesting weak evidence, which did not improve substantially when more sensitive ranges were used.
evidence: This is a result from Bayes factor analysis.

claim: When both MCI and AD groups were combined, BF increased to 13.70 for slow gamma (26–34 Hz) and 8.60 for fast gamma (44–56 Hz).
source: However, when both MCI and AD groups were combined, BF increased to 13.70 for slow gamma (26–34 Hz) and 8.60 for fast gamma (44–56 Hz), further strengthening the evidence in favor of alternate hypothesis.
evidence: This is a result from Bayes factor analysis for the combined group.

claim: Evidence for alpha band power was in favor of the null hypothesis (BF was 0.088 when only MCIs were considered, 0.29 for ADs, and 0.077 when both MCI and AD subjects were considered).
source: On the other hand, evidence for alpha band power was in favor of the null hypothesis (BF was 0.088 when only MCIs were considered, 0.29 for ADs, and 0.077 when both MCI and AD subjects were considered).
evidence: This is a result from Bayes factor analysis for alpha power.

claim: Previous studies have correlated increases in gamma power with occurrence of microsaccades.
source: Previous studies have correlated increases in gamma power with occurrence of small involuntary eye movements called microsaccades (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls had comparable eye positions and microsaccade profiles.
source: We compared eye data between MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls and found comparable eye positions and microsaccade profiles (Figure 4A), similar main sequence (Figure 4B), and similar pupillary reactivity (Figure 4C) to stimulus presentation (measured as coefficient of variation of pupil diameter across time; see Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eye tracking data presented in Figure 4.

claim: MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls had similar main sequence.
source: We compared eye data between MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls and found comparable eye positions and microsaccade profiles (Figure 4A), similar main sequence (Figure 4B), and similar pupillary reactivity (Figure 4C) to stimulus presentation (measured as coefficient of variation of pupil diameter across time; see Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eye tracking data presented in Figure 4.

claim: MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls had similar pupillary reactivity to stimulus presentation.
source: We compared eye data between MCI/AD subjects and their respective controls and found comparable eye positions and microsaccade profiles (Figure 4A), similar main sequence (Figure 4B), and similar pupillary reactivity (Figure 4C) to stimulus presentation (measured as coefficient of variation of pupil diameter across time; see Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eye tracking data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The cases (MCIs or ADs) and their respective controls had comparable PSDs in the baseline condition.
source: The cases (MCIs or ADs) and their respective controls had comparable PSDs (Figure 5) and slopes of PSDs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) in the baseline condition.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of baseline data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Baseline power in alpha, slow gamma, and fast gamma frequency ranges did not differ significantly between cases and controls.
source: Further, baseline power in alpha, slow gamma, and fast gamma frequency ranges did not differ significantly between cases and controls (K-W test; for MCIs: χ2(23) = 0.48/0/0, p=0.49/0.95/1 for alpha/slow/fast gamma, respectively; for AD: χ2(9) = 0.27/0.53/0.27, p=0.60/0.46/0.60 for alpha/slow/fast gamma, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: SSVEP power at 32 Hz was comparable in MCI and control groups (K-W Test, χ2(13) = 0.04, p=0.85).
source: We did not observe any reduction in SSVEP power at 32 Hz in the MCI group as compared to the control group (K-W Test, significance at each frequency of the change in power spectra is shown in Figure 6A; significance at 32 Hz: χ2(13) = 0.04, p=0.85).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with specific statistical values.

claim: This is the first study to find abnormalities in visual narrow-band gamma oscillations elicited by Cartesian gratings in human EEG in MCI and AD.
source: However, this is the first study to our knowledge that found abnormalities in visual narrow-band gamma oscillations elicited by Cartesian gratings in human EEG in MCI and AD.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: van Deursen et al., 2008 examined neural activity in gamma frequency range and found that gamma activity increased in subjects with MCI/AD.
source: Previously, van Deursen et al., 2008 examined neural activity in gamma frequency range and found that gamma activity increased in subjects with MCI/AD, as opposed to their initially proposed hypothesis.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from a cited study.

claim: The study's findings are different from van Deursen et al., 2008, probably due to differences in task settings.
source: Our findings are different from theirs, probably due to the differences in task settings: we had tested for visual gamma rhythms induced by gratings, whereas they had tested for resting-state gamma as well as gamma activity for multiple-colored objects randomly moving on a computer screen (taken from screensavers).
evidence: This is an inference about why the results differ from prior work.

claim: The sample is representative of urban population in India as the study adopted community-based sampling instead of hospital-based sampling.
source: Our sample is a representative of urban population in India as we adopted community-based sampling instead of hospital-based sampling.
evidence: This is a claim about the representativeness of the sample based on the sampling method.

claim: Out of the 257 subjects that data was collected from, there were 13 MCIs (~5%) and 6 AD subjects (2.3%).
source: Importantly, out of the 257 subjects that we collected data from (247 used for analysis plus 10 subjects whose data was noisy and thus rejected, see 'Materials and methods'), there were 13 MCIs (~5%) and 6 AD subjects (2.3%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the sample composition.

claim: The prevalence of MCI and AD in the study sample matches closely to the previously reported prevalence of MCI and AD in India.
source: These figures match closely to the previously reported prevalence of MCI and AD in India (Kalaria et al., 2008; Mathuranath et al., 2012; Sosa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior epidemiological data supported by citations.

claim: Within the recruited sample, most cases (~70%) had MCI.
source: Within the recruited sample, most cases (~70%) had MCI, a condition that is conceptualized as intermediate stage between normal aging and AD.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the sample composition.

claim: MCI is conceptualized as intermediate stage between normal aging and AD.
source: Within the recruited sample, most cases (~70%) had MCI, a condition that is conceptualized as intermediate stage between normal aging and AD.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge.

claim: Criteria used to diagnose MCI are not strong and hence there is a need for a valid biomarker.
source: Criteria used to diagnose MCI are not strong and hence there is a need for a valid biomarker.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current diagnostic criteria.

claim: The study highlights the potential use of gamma oscillations in EEG as a biomarker for MCI.
source: Our study highlights the potential use of gamma oscillations in EEG in that direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential application of the findings.

claim: The study limited analyses to sensor (electrode) level instead of reconstructing the neural sources.
source: Moreover, we had limited our analyses to sensor (electrode) level instead of reconstructing the neural sources and performing analyses at that level.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the study.

claim: Limiting analyses to sensor level has allowed the study to present a screening technique that is easy to replicate in a clinical setting.
source: This has allowed us to present a screening technique that is easy to replicate in a clinical setting.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of the methodological choice.

claim: The study's metrics were derived directly from neural activity and could serve as a more objective assessment of the clinical status of the individual.
source: Furthermore, as our metrics were derived directly from neural activity, these could serve as a more objective assessment of the clinical status of the individual.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential advantage of the biomarker.

claim: Gamma rhythms are generated by excitatory-inhibitory interactions in the brain.
source: Gamma rhythms are generated by excitatory-inhibitory interactions in the brain (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Excitatory-inhibitory interactions could be influenced by many structural factors that could get abnormal in AD (such as cortical thinning and atrophy).
source: These interactions could be influenced by many structural factors (Buzsáki et al., 2013) that could get abnormal in AD (such as cortical thinning and atrophy; see Dickerson et al., 2009; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: How structural derailments in AD influence gamma recorded over scalp is unknown.
source: However, how such structural derailments influence gamma recorded over scalp is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: A few studies in MEG had reported significant positive correlations between gamma frequency and cortical thickness as well as volume of cuneus.
source: A few studies in MEG had reported significant positive correlations between gamma frequency and cortical thickness as well as volume of cuneus (Gaetz et al., 2012) and thickness of pericalcarine area (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Correlations between gamma frequency and cortical structure could not be replicated in later studies and have been shown to be confounded by age.
source: However, such results could not be replicated in later studies (Cousijn et al., 2014) and have been shown to be confounded by age (Robson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Age is a common factor that influences both macroscopic structure and gamma power and frequency.
source: Age is as a common factor that influences both macroscopic structure (Lemaitre et al., 2012; Salat et al., 2004; van Pelt et al., 2018) as well as gamma power and frequency (Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Structural changes in AD brain are more evident and drastic compared to cognitively healthy aging.
source: However, as structural changes in AD brain are more evident and drastic compared to cognitively healthy aging (Dickerson et al., 2009; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2011), future studies should examine correlations of gamma power/frequency and macroscopic structure such as cortical thickness in healthy/MCI/AD subjects while controlling for age.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some investigators have suggested neuroprotective effects of entraining neural oscillations using flickering light/sound at 40 Hz in rodent models of AD.
source: Some investigators have suggested neuroprotective effects of entraining neural oscillations using flickering light/sound at 40 Hz (analogous to our SSVEP paradigm) in rodent models of AD (Adaikkan et al., 2019; Martorell et al., 2019; Thomson, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study did not find any significant trend for SSVEP at 32 Hz in cases compared to controls.
source: Although we did not find any significant trend for SSVEP at 32 Hz in cases compared to controls (unlike our observations with narrow-band gamma), we cannot directly compare the results from abovementioned studies with our study for several reasons.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's findings regarding SSVEPs.

claim: The frequency of entrainment was different between the study (32 Hz) and prior rodent studies (40 Hz).
source: First, the frequency of entrainment was different (40 Hz vs 32 Hz).
evidence: This is a methodological difference noted by the authors.

claim: The model organism was different between the study (human) and prior studies (rodent).
source: Second, the model organism was different (human vs rodent).
evidence: This is a methodological difference noted by the authors.

claim: The study did not measure any cognitive or pathological outcome of the visual stimulation.
source: Finally, we did not measure any cognitive or pathological outcome of the visual stimulation.
evidence: This is a statement about what the study did not measure.

claim: It is possible that entrainment of neural oscillations to visual stimulation in gamma frequency range gets deranged only in advanced stages of AD.
source: It is possible that entrainment of neural oscillations to visual stimulation in gamma frequency range gets deranged only in advanced stages of AD (as in the rodent models of Iaccarino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible explanation for the findings.

claim: Entrainment may have therapeutic benefit but may not reflect as abnormal on testing early on.
source: It may thus have therapeutic benefit but may not reflect as abnormal on testing early on (as in our case).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible explanation for the findings.

claim: The differences in trends for gratings and SSVEP evoked gamma suggest that these two phenomena might be sub-served by different, yet unknown mechanisms.
source: Nonetheless, the differences in trends for gratings and SSVEP evoked gamma presented in this study suggest that these two phenomena might be sub-served by different, yet unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrasting results for gratings and SSVEPs.

claim: Stimulus-induced change in visual narrow-band gamma power has the potential to be a simple, low-cost, easy to replicate, and objective biomarker for screening of MCI and AD.
source: Stimulus-induced change in visual narrow-band gamma power has the potential to be a simple, low-cost, easy to replicate, and objective biomarker for screening of MCI and AD.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential application of the findings.

claim: How the gamma-based biomarker compares against other methods used in diagnosis (MRI, PET, cognitive tests, etc.) remains an open question.
source: How this gamma-based biomarker compares against other methods used in diagnosis (MRI, PET, cognitive tests, etc.), whether addition of this biomarker to other standard methods improves the overall diagnosis, and the specificity of this biomarker for AD compared to other causes of dementia remain open questions that will require further research.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations and future research directions.

claim: Whether addition of the gamma-based biomarker to other standard methods improves the overall diagnosis remains an open question.
source: How this gamma-based biomarker compares against other methods used in diagnosis (MRI, PET, cognitive tests, etc.), whether addition of this biomarker to other standard methods improves the overall diagnosis, and the specificity of this biomarker for AD compared to other causes of dementia remain open questions that will require further research.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations and future research directions.

claim: The specificity of the gamma-based biomarker for AD compared to other causes of dementia remains an open question.
source: How this gamma-based biomarker compares against other methods used in diagnosis (MRI, PET, cognitive tests, etc.), whether addition of this biomarker to other standard methods improves the overall diagnosis, and the specificity of this biomarker for AD compared to other causes of dementia remain open questions that will require further research.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations and future research directions.

claim: The study recruited 257 elderly subjects (109 females) aged 50–92 years from the Tata Longitudinal Study of Aging (TLSA) cohort from urban communities in Bangalore between July 2016 and July 2019.
source: We recruited 257 elderly subjects (109 females) aged 50–92 years from the Tata Longitudinal Study of Aging (TLSA) cohort from urban communities in Bangalore between July 2016 and July 2019.
evidence: This describes the study's recruitment details.

claim: Subjects were clinically diagnosed by psychiatrists and/or a neurologist as cognitively healthy (N = 236) or suffering from MCI (N = 15) or AD (N = 6) through clinical history and a semi-structured clinical interview (Clinical Dementia Rating).
source: They were clinically diagnosed by psychiatrists (authors BN/AML) and/or a neurologist (author MJ) as cognitively healthy (N = 236) or suffering from MCI (N = 15) or AD (N = 6) through clinical history and a semi-structured clinical interview (Clinical Dementia Rating; see Table 1).
evidence: This describes the diagnostic process used in the study.

claim: Five out of the six AD subjects were directly referred to the study by the neurologist.
source: Five out of the six AD subjects were directly referred to the study by the neurologist.
evidence: This describes how some AD subjects were recruited.

claim: Diagnosis of all MCI/AD subjects was further reviewed by a panel of four experts for consensus.
source: Diagnosis of all MCI/AD subjects was further reviewed by a panel of four experts for consensus (see Appendix; criteria used by the panel are given in Tables 1–3 in Supplementary file 1), who reclassified two MCI subjects as healthy.
evidence: This describes an additional diagnostic review process.

claim: A panel of four experts reclassified two MCI subjects as healthy.
source: Diagnosis of all MCI/AD subjects was further reviewed by a panel of four experts for consensus (see Appendix; criteria used by the panel are given in Tables 1–3 in Supplementary file 1), who reclassified two MCI subjects as healthy.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the diagnostic review.

claim: The study recorded raw EEG signals from 64 active electrodes using BrainAmp DC according to the international 10–10 system, referenced online at FCz.
source: Briefly, we recorded raw EEG signals from 64 active electrodes using BrainAmp DC (Brain Products GmbH, Germany) according to the international 10–10 system, referenced online at FCz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording setup.

claim: Raw EEG signals were filtered online between 0.016 Hz and 1000 Hz and sampled at 2500 Hz.
source: We filtered raw signals online between 0.016 Hz and 1000 Hz and sampled at 2500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG signal processing parameters.

claim: Electrodes whose impedance was more than 25 KΩ were rejected (4.0%, 3.4%, and 0.6% for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, respectively).
source: We rejected electrodes whose impedance was more than 25 KΩ (4.0%, 3.4%, and 0.6% for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, respectively).
evidence: This describes the electrode quality control criteria.

claim: Impedance of the final set of electrodes was 5.5 ± 4.2, 5.9 ± 4.4, and 3.8 ± 3.5 KΩ for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, respectively.
source: Impedance of the final set of electrodes was 5.5 ± 4.2, 5.9 ± 4.4, and 3.8 ± 3.5 KΩ for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of electrode impedance.

claim: The screen was gamma-corrected and placed at a mean ± SD distance of 58.1 ± 0.8 cm from the subjects.
source: The screen (BenQ XL2411, resolution 1280 × 720 pixels, refresh rate 100 Hz) was gamma-corrected and placed at a mean ± SD distance of 58.1 ± 0.8 cm from the subjects (53.8–61.0 cm) according to their convenience (thus subtending a width of at least 52° and height of at least 30° of visual field for full-screen gratings).
evidence: This describes the visual display setup.

claim: The study chose 32 Hz SSVEP (induced by gratings of temporal frequency of 16 cycles per second) because the SSVEP gain was highest for gratings with temporal frequencies of 12-16 cps in a separate set of experiments in awake monkeys.
source: We chose 32 Hz SSVEP (induced by gratings of temporal frequency of 16 cycles per second or cps) for two reasons. First, in a separate set of experiments, we had recorded spikes and local field potentials (LFP) in the primary visual cortex of awake monkeys while presenting counterphasing gratings at varying temporal frequencies and found that the SSVEP gain was highest for gratings with temporal frequencies of 12-16 cps (Salelkar and Ray, 2020).
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing the SSVEP frequency based on prior experiments.

claim: 32 Hz was chosen for SSVEP because it was between slow and fast gamma bands.
source: Second, 32 Hz was between slow and fast gamma bands, hence within the available time for the experiment, we were able to record SSVEP activity closest to both the gamma rhythms.
evidence: This explains another rationale for choosing the SSVEP frequency.

claim: The study recorded eye signals (pupil position and diameter data) using EyeLink 1000 for all subjects (except for one subject each in healthy/MCI/AD categories).
source: We recorded eye signals (pupil position and diameter data) using EyeLink 1000 (SR Research Ltd) for all subjects (except for one subject each in healthy/MCI/AD categories).
evidence: This describes the eye tracking setup.

claim: Stimulus repeats with fixation breaks (eye blinks or shifts in eye position outside a square window of width 5° centered on the fixation spot) during −0.5 s to 0.75 s of stimulus onset were rejected.
source: We rejected stimulus repeats with fixation breaks (eye blinks or shifts in eye position outside a square window of width 5° centered on the fixation spot) during −0.5 s to 0.75 s of stimulus onset (mean ± SD: 16.7 ± 14.2%, 12.8 ± 12%, and 31.6 ± 18.4% for Gamma experiment; and 16.7 ± 15.1%, 9.1 ± 16%, and 46.4 ± 1% for SSVEP experiment, for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, respectively).
evidence: This describes the criteria for rejecting trials based on eye movements.

claim: All subjects were able to maintain fixation with a standard deviation of less than 0.5°, 0.3°, and 0.6° for Gamma experiment and 0.6°, 0.4°, 0.6° for SSVEP experiment for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, in either directions.
source: For the remaining repeats, all the subjects were able to maintain fixation with a standard deviation of less than 0.5°, 0.3°, and 0.6° for Gamma experiment and 0.6°, 0.4°, 0.6° for SSVEP experiment for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, in either directions.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of fixation stability.

claim: The study used a pipeline to reject artifact-containing data as described in Murty et al., 2020.
source: We used a pipeline to reject artifact-containing data as described in Murty et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the artifact rejection method.

claim: The study discarded those electrodes that had more than 30% of all repeats marked as bad.
source: We discarded those electrodes that had more than 30% of all repeats marked as bad, and subsequently labelled any repeat as bad if it occurred in more than 10% of total number of remaining electrodes.
evidence: This describes the criteria for discarding electrodes.

claim: The study discarded any block that did not have at least a single clean bipolar electrode pair in any of three specified groups of bipolar electrodes.
source: Further, we discarded any block that did not have at least a single clean bipolar electrode pair (see Data Analysis subsection below) in any of the following three groups of bipolar electrodes: PO3-P1, PO3-P3, POz-PO3; PO4-P2, PO4-P4, POz-PO4 and Oz-POz, Oz-O1, Oz-O2.
evidence: This describes the criteria for discarding blocks.

claim: The study rejected 53/497, 4/31, and 1/15 blocks for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects.
source: Despite these strict criteria, we ended up rejecting only 53/497, 4/31, and 1/15 blocks for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects; and we rejected only 5.5 ± 6.4%, 5.7 ± 3.6%, and 4.1 ± 1.9% of electrodes for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, among those blocks that were analyzed.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of data rejection.

claim: The study rejected only 5.5 ± 6.4%, 5.7 ± 3.6%, and 4.1 ± 1.9% of electrodes for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, among those blocks that were analyzed.
source: Despite these strict criteria, we ended up rejecting only 53/497, 4/31, and 1/15 blocks for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects; and we rejected only 5.5 ± 6.4%, 5.7 ± 3.6%, and 4.1 ± 1.9% of electrodes for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, among those blocks that were analyzed.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of electrode rejection.

claim: The study discarded 9 of 236 healthy subjects and 1 of 15 MCIs from further analysis because they did not have any analyzable blocks.
source: Those subjects who did not have any analyzable blocks (9 of 236 healthy subjects and 1 of 15 MCIs, respectively) were discarded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes subject exclusion criteria.

claim: For the SSVEP experiment, the study rejected 25/222, 5/12, and 3/5 blocks for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects.
source: Consequently, we rejected 25/222, 5/12, and 3/5 blocks for healthy, MCI, and AD subjects; and 6.6 ± 7.2%, 8.5 ± 7.4%, and 5.7 ± 1% of electrodes among those blocks that were analyzed.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of data rejection for the SSVEP experiment.

claim: For the SSVEP experiment, the study rejected data from 25/4/3 out of 222/11/5 subjects as they did not have any analyzable blocks, leaving 197/7/2 healthy/MCI/AD subjects for analysis.
source: Hence, we rejected data from 25/4/3 out of 222/11/5 subjects as they did not have any analyzable blocks, leaving 197/7/2 (93/1/1 females) healthy/MCI/AD subjects for analysis for the SSVEP experiment.
evidence: This describes subject exclusion for the SSVEP experiment.

claim: The study re-referenced data at each electrode offline to its neighboring electrodes (bipolar reference), obtaining 112 bipolar pairs out of 64 unipolar electrodes.
source: For all analyses we re-referenced data at each electrode offline to its neighboring electrodes (bipolar reference). We thus obtained 112 bipolar pairs out of 64 unipolar electrodes (Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the re-referencing method used in the analysis.

claim: The study considered nine bipolar electrodes for analysis: PO3-P1, PO3-P3, POz-PO3, PO4-P2, PO4-P4, POz-PO4, Oz-POz, Oz-O1, Oz-O2.
source: We considered the following nine bipolar electrodes for analysis: PO3-P1, PO3-P3, POz-PO3, PO4-P2, PO4-P4, POz-PO4, Oz-POz, Oz-O1, Oz-O2, which are inside the black encapsulation shown in Figure 2D.
evidence: This describes the electrode selection for analysis.

claim: The study computed PSD and time-frequency power spectrograms using multi-taper method with a single taper using Chronux toolbox.
source: We computed PSD and the time-frequency power spectrograms using multi-taper method with a single taper using Chronux toolbox (Mitra and Bokil, 2008; http://chronux.org/, RRID:SCR_005547).
evidence: This describes the spectral analysis method.

claim: The study chose baseline period between −500 ms and 0 ms of stimulus onset, and stimulus period between 250 ms and 750 ms, to avoid stimulus onset-related transients.
source: We chose baseline period between −500 ms and 0 ms of stimulus onset, and stimulus period between 250 ms and 750 ms, to avoid stimulus onset-related transients, yielding a frequency resolution of 2 Hz for the PSDs.
evidence: This describes the time windows used for analysis.

claim: The study detected microsaccades using a threshold-based method initially proposed by Engbert, 2006.
source: We detected microsaccades using a threshold-based method described earlier (Murty et al., 2018), initially proposed by Engbert, 2006, for the analysis period of −0.5 s to 0.75 s of stimulus onset for the Gamma experiment.
evidence: This describes the microsaccade detection method.

claim: The study used coefficient of variation (CV, ratio of standard deviation to mean) of pupil diameter across time for every repeat as a measure of pupillary reactivity to stimulus for that repeat.
source: We used coefficient of variation (CV, ratio of standard deviation to mean) of pupil diameter across time for every repeat as a measure of pupillary reactivity to stimulus for that repeat (Murty et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the pupil reactivity measure.

claim: All statistical interpretations were based on non-parametric tests on medians using K-W test.
source: All our statistical interpretations were based on non-parametric tests on medians using K-W test (results were similar if we used Wilcoxon sign-rank test).
evidence: This describes the statistical testing approach.

claim: The study used two-way ANOVA for comparing change in alpha/gamma power across spatial frequencies and orientations for 227 healthy subjects.
source: We used two-way ANOVA for comparing change in alpha/gamma power across spatial frequencies and orientations for 227 healthy subjects (see Results section).
evidence: This describes a specific statistical test used.

claim: The study is controlled at p<0.05 regardless of the sample size, since the false alarm rate does not depend on the sample size.
source: The study is controlled at p<0.05 regardless of the sample size, since the false alarm rate does not depend on the sample size.
evidence: This describes the statistical significance threshold.
